entries.name: Log cabin
entries.purpose: dwelling, farm and woodcutter's house, hunting lodge
parts: horizontal log walls with notched corners
gabled timber roof
stone or brick chimney (later)
loft under the roof
small windows
layout: one rectangular room, often with a loft
door on a gable end, south-facing preferred
hearth or stove at one end

entries.found: forested Europe and North America; single homesteads scattered through clearings, small hamlets at the frontier
entries.notes: The seed of frontier building: easy to raise from local timber with an axe. A single-pen cabin is one room; later settlers joined two pens with a breezeway (dogtrot).

entries.name: Thatched cottage
materials: lime-washed wattle and daub or brick
wheat straw or water reed thatch
entries.purpose: dwelling for farming families and labourers
parts: steeply pitched thatched roof with deep eaves
thick insulating walls
small casement windows
brick or stone chimney
low lintel, thick door
layout: one room deep, main door off-centre
main room downstairs, bedrooms in the roof or a lean-to
cottage garden and often a pigsty behind
entries.found: rural England, Ireland and northern France; surviving density highest in the south and east of England
entries.notes: Deep eaves and steep pitch are the whole silhouette. Fire is the enemy: chimneys need spark guards and the thatch must stay sound.

entries.name: Stone cottage (Cotswold cottage)
entries.purpose: dwelling, often handloom weaver's cottage in earlier centuries
parts: honey-coloured limestone walls
steep roof of split limestone slabs
mullioned windows
arched or square door, often off-centre
stone boundary walls (dry stone or mortared)
layout: two storeys plus attic
room width shed, small and dark inside
garden walled in the same stone
entries.found: the Cotswold Hills and surrounding limestone country of central-south England
entries.notes: Instantly readable regional marker; the whole village turns one colour of stone. Roofs lose their stone slates fastest, so sagging ridge lines are common.

entries.name: Half-timbered house (fachwerk / Tudor)
materials: wattle and daub or brick infill
entries.purpose: urban and village dwelling, often with shop or workshop below
parts: exposed dark timber frame with pale infill panels
jettying (upper floors overhang the street)
steep roof
carved bargeboards or gable decorations
small latticed windows
layout: ground floor: shop/workshop and entry; upper floors: living rooms
jetties supported on carved brackets
narrow gable end to the street
entries.found: old town centres of Germany, Switzerland, Normandy, Picardy, the Low Countries and England
entries.notes: Upper storeys lean over the street to claim more floor area without widening the parcel — great for dense medieval blocks. Black tarred beams against white plaster is the classic read.

entries.name: Saltbox (colonial house)
entries.purpose: dwelling for settler farm families
parts: asymmetric pitched roof sweeping long over the rear
central chimney
two storeys in front, one at the rear
clapboard or shingle cladding
small multi-pane sash windows
layout: four rooms per floor around a central chimney stack
parlour and kitchen down, chambers up
added rear lean-to under the long roof slope
entries.found: New England, especially eastern Massachusetts and Connecticut
entries.notes: Gabled like a saltbox for keeping tea in — the name fits the shape exactly. The one-storey rear extension was added as families grew, under the extended back roof.

entries.name: Izba
entries.purpose: dwelling for peasant farming families
parts: horizontal log walls
massive Russian stove (pech) in the rear corner
sleeping bench on the stove (polati)
steep timber roof, chimneyless at first (smoke out through the door)
small windows
layout: one large room (gornitsa) around the stove
stove occupies a rear corner, its hot mass radiates for hours
loft above for storage, entry porch in front
entries.found: rural Russia and Ukraine; preserved widely in open-air museums near Moscow and Novgorod
entries.notes: The whitewashed clay stove is the whole house: bread baking, water heating, sleeping perch and smoke-drying of laundry all happened on or around it. A single window warmed rarely; smoke rolled along the eaves.

entries.name: Terraced (row) house, Georgian to Victorian
entries.purpose: urban dwelling for artisans, clerks and, later, factory workers
parts: three to four storeys with shared party walls
basement or cellar sometimes
pitched slate roof with party-wall gables
sash windows, often uniformly spaced
small rear yard and outbuilding
layout: cellar: storage/coal, ground floor: front parlour and back kitchen
upper floors: bedrooms; attic under the roof
stair near the middle, rooms front and back
entries.found: London's inner districts and the industrial cities (Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool); packed along straight streets
entries.notes: The default English urban house of the industrial era. Identical plots, identical brickwork — the variety is in door colour and window rhythm, not the form.

entries.name: Brownstone (rowhouse)
entries.purpose: urban middle-class town dwelling
parts: raised stoop entrance above a garden level
front parlour and rear parlour/dining
upper bedroom floors
flat roof with cornice
areaway moat/railing at the front
layout: stoop leads to a raised piano nobile; street level holds kitchen and service rooms
front parlour for company, back for dining
small rear extension for bath and kitchen
entries.found: Brooklyn, Manhattan, Philadelphia, Baltimore — middle-class districts near transit
entries.notes: A facade of carved brownstone pretending to be a private mansion. The stoop is the social theatre of the block: everyone passes it.

entries.name: Minka (farmhouse)
entries.purpose: dwelling of farmers, artisans and merchants
parts: deep pitched irimoya roof
doma (earthen-floor work area)
raised hiroma/zashiki living area (tatami in richer houses)
irori (sunken hearth) with jizai-kagi hook
engawa veranda under the eaves (in some regions)
layout: doma at one end for animals, tools and work; raised woon area at the other
four rooms (yomadori) off the doma side in the standard plan
irori at the centre of family life; loft above for sericulture or storage
entries.found: rural Japan; regional styles (honmune, gassho) differ by mountain basin and snow load
entries.notes: Smoke rises through the roof, no chimney — it seasons the timber and keeps pests down. Richer farmhouses are hard to distinguish from minor samurai houses at a glance.

entries.name: Gasshō-zukuri farmhouse
entries.purpose: dwelling of plain-mountain farm families, silk work on upper floors
parts: gable roof at 45–60 degrees, two hands clasped in prayer
open sasu-beam framework, rope-lashed
large central room around the irori
sericulture lofts above, two to three storeys
steep gable ends with suzume-odori decoration (in honmune style)
layout: steep roof sheds 3–4 m of annual snow
earth floor at one end, raised tatami living area at the other
upper floors: mulberry-fed silkworm trays and storage
entries.found: Shirakawa-gō (Gifu) and Gokayama (Toyama); UNESCO World Heritage villages
entries.notes: The most extreme thatched roof in Japan: a living triangle that lets snow and rain run straight off. Communal repair every 20–30 years is a village event.

entries.name: Hanok
entries.purpose: dwelling of yangban gentry, and later commoners
parts: giwa roof with gentle upward-curving eaves
maru (timber-floored hall) in the middle
ondol rooms with underfloor hot-air heating on both sides
madang (central open courtyard)
cheoma (curved eave corners)
layout: rooms on both sides of the maru, courtyard in front
kitchen and ondol firebox at one end
gate wall with screen against views into the compound
entries.found: Seoul (Bukchon), Jeonju, Andong (Hahoe village); most common in the central and southern provinces
entries.notes: Underfloor ondol heating radiates from firebed chambers under the rooms — the original Korean radiant floor. Gently curved roof lines are its signature against straight Chinese roofs.

entries.name: Swiss chalet (alpine farmhouse)
entries.purpose: dwelling and barn combined for summer pasture farming
parts: broad eaves far beyond the walls
carved balconies and bargeboards
stone ground floor (cows and stores), timber upper floors (family)
steep pitched shingle roof
small square windows with shutters
layout: livestock and hay below, family above
gable end faces the valley
wide balcony on the gable end catches morning sun
entries.found: Alpine valleys of Switzerland, Savoy, Vorarlberg and the Alto Adige; romanticized worldwide by 19th-century books
entries.notes: The wide eaves are the structure's argument against heavy snow: they throw melting water well clear of the timber walls. Deeply carved decoration marked the owner's prosperity.

entries.name: Irish vernacular cottage
materials: stone or unplastered mud walls (white-washed with lime)
entries.purpose: dwelling of tenant farmers and cottiers
parts: thick insulating walls
thatched gabled roof
very small windows (a light tax was abolished in 1851)
half-door opening in summer
open hearth in the main room
layout: single-storey; rooms in a line: byre or store, main room, bedrooms
gable end to the road, door facing the yard
hearth in the centre of the main room
entries.found: all over rural Ireland; densest in the west and south-west
entries.notes: Window tax explains the pinholes: walls two feet thick, windows the size of plates. Many were limewashed white, many others left in raw grey rubble stone.

entries.name: Domus (Roman townhouse)
entries.purpose: dwelling of a wealthy urban household with its slaves and clients
parts: street-front with two shops (tabernae) flanking the entrance
atrium with compluvium (open roof) and impluvium (rain basin)
tablinum (master's office, open to both)
peristyle garden behind
cubicula (bedrooms), triclinium (dining room)
layout: axial plan: door → atrium → tablinum → peristyle
dark, formal front; private, bright, green rear
cave (inner garden) is off-axis, screened for family
entries.found: Roman cities, best preserved at Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia
entries.notes: Not built on a grid: one deep axial line from street door to garden, flanked symmetrically by rooms. A domus at Pompeii was a statement of lineage and self-control.

entries.name: Roman villa
entries.purpose: seat of a large country estate, residence of the owner and management hub of the farm
parts: peristyle courtyard
bath suite (caldarium, tepidarium, frigidarium)
oecus (reception hall)
mosaic floors
colonnades and gardens
estate wing (pars rustica): barns, press, slaves' quarters
layout: central courtyard, rooms arranged in wings
villa urbana (the family wing) separated from pars rustica (farm)
often outward-looking colonnades toward cultivated land
entries.found: across the Roman world; Italy, Gaul, Britain, Hispania, North Africa, Pannonia
entries.notes: A villa is half mansion, half farm HQ. Identity signals: bath suite size, mosaic quality, number of colonnades. Rich villas had sea views or faced south.

entries.name: Insula (Roman apartment block)
entries.purpose: rental housing for ordinary citizens — most Romans lived here, not in a domus
parts: ground floor shops (tabernae) with living space above
four to six rental apartments above
internal staircase(s)
sometimes a small courtyard or lightwell
street-facing balconies in better blocks
layout: commercial ground floor, residential above
top-floor rooms cheapest and smallest
often inward-facing around a narrow court
entries.found: dense Roman cities: Ostia, Rome, Carthage, Pompeii (rare), Herculaneum (preserved)
entries.notes: Height regulations capped insulae at roughly 18–21 m. Fire and collapse were constant hazards — hence Augustus's and Trajan's building-height laws, and the preference to live low.

entries.name: Siheyuan (courtyard house)
entries.purpose: multi-generational family compound of officials, merchants and scholars
parts: entrance gate (usually southeast), sometimes with a screen wall
central open courtyard (yardan)
main hall on the north side (head of family)
east and west wings (sons and guests)
small flower/rock/tree centrepiece in the yard
layout: walled compound, rooms turned inward to the courtyard
hierarchy by position: north is most honoured, parents in the main hall
wings face the courtyard; children and servants on the sides
entries.found: Beijing and the North China Plain; destroyed en masse by 20th-century redevelopment
entries.notes: A fortress turned family: everyone turns inward, nobody sees in from the street. The courtyard is the living room of the whole compound.

entries.name: Black Forest farmhouse (Schwarzwaldhaus)
entries.purpose: one-roof farmhouse: livestock, hay, barn and family dwelling together
parts: very steep roof descending almost to the ground
open hall (Rauchküche) in historic houses — no chimney
barn integrated at one end
deep eaves, often white-trimmed gables
large wooden gate to the farmyard
layout: cows below, family above in older examples
single entrance from the farmyard into the Rauchküche
lofts under the roof store hay and grain
entries.found: the Black Forest (Schwarzwald) of southwest Germany; also scattered in the Vosges and northern foothills
entries.notes: The roof is the house: one huge dark triangle with walls tucked beneath. Historic versions had no chimney; smoke from the central hearth cured the timber and hung bacon in the rafters.

entries.name: Blackhouse (taigh dubh)
materials: double drystone walls filled with earth and stones
entries.purpose: dwelling and byre combined for tenant crofting families
parts: very thick double drystone walls with an earth core
byre at one end, sharing a partition with the family end
open peat hearth in the middle; no chimney in early forms
clay floor, often flagstones
no internal subdivisions
layout: long rectangle; cattle at one end, family and fire at the other, corn in between
people and livestock under one roof for warmth
door at the gable end off the yard
entries.found: Scottish Highlands and Islands; best preserved on Lewis and Harris and in open-air museums
entries.notes: The name comes from the dark interior — smoke-filled, no windows to speak of. A family and a cow shared the same shelter; the heat difference kept both alive.

entries.name: Khata (whitewashed cottage)
materials: wattle and daub or brick, whitewashed outside
entries.purpose: dwelling of peasant farming families
parts: whitewashed walls
thatched hipped roof with low pitch
small windows
painted trim around windows and door (folk ornament)
pich (clay stove) in the rear wall
layout: single storey; rooms in a row: porch, main room, cold storage
stove in the corner, bench along the back wall
front garden (flowers, sunflowers) before the door
entries.found: rural Ukraine and parts of southern Poland
entries.notes: The white cube with a thatched hat and sunflowers in the yard — the iconic image of the Ukrainian countryside. Interiors were painted and ornamented with regional motifs.

entries.name: Baserri (Basque farmhouse)
entries.purpose: family farm dwelling and agricultural headquarters in the same building
parts: massive roof sweeping low to shelter the upper floors
stone base (livestock and stores) with timber upper storeys (family)
big carved wooden balcony or arcade
single large gate to the farmyard
layout: ground floor: cattle, hay, press and stores; upper floors: family rooms
orientation adapted to slope; big gable facing the valley
farm buildings continue the family lineage for generations
entries.found: Basque Country (Euskal Herria), Spain and France
entries.notes: A baserri is an ancient family estate, often with a single family name attached for centuries — land, house and lineage are one word in Basque (etxe). Many have been converted into apartments and still bear the name boards.

entries.name: Masia (Catalan farmhouse)
entries.purpose: family farm dwelling and agricultural headquarters
parts: thick stone walls
gabled tile roof, often very large
sometimes a defensive tower (torre) attached
big central door, arched or square
attached farm outbuildings (premsas, stables)
layout: central hall (entrada) with rooms off it; animals and press below or behind
family above; loft under the roof for grain and hay
water cistern and dovecote often beside the house
entries.found: Catalonia and the Balearic Islands
entries.notes: The masia is the centre of the Catalan countryside the way the baserri is for the Basque lands. Towers are real defensive features from the centuries of coastal raiding.

entries.name: Mas (Provençal farmhouse)
entries.purpose: family farm dwelling of a mixed arable–sheep–vine estate
parts: massive stone walls
tiled pitched roof
small windows with wooden shutters
tower or dovecote (status)
cistern and well close by
layout: ground floor: press, cellar, animals; upper floors: family rooms
facade toward the farmyard, living rooms on the sunny side
vines, olives and garrigue right up to the walls
entries.found: Provence and Languedoc, southern France
entries.notes: A fortified farm, not a villa: walls 60 cm thick, tiny windows, deep roof. Many are now guesthouses and wineries; the best still press wine on the ground floor.

entries.name: Cycladic house (whitewashed cube)
materials: rubble stone, lime plaster, limewash white
blue paint (modern, for doors and shutters)
entries.purpose: dwelling of island farmer–sailor–fisher families
parts: cubic white volumes stacked up the slope
flat or slightly domed roof (roof terrace)
tiny deep-set windows
blue door and shutter accents (20th c.)
external staircase to a roof terrace
layout: rooms piled one on another up the hill, sharing party walls
lower room (animal/stores), upper room (family), stair outside
alley roofs open to the sky — the street itself is sometimes the ceiling
entries.found: the Cyclades islands (Mykonos, Santorini, Paros, Naxos)
entries.notes: Whitewash deflects the sun and disinfects with lime. The whole village reads as one continuous white sculpture; wind and salt beat everything metal.

entries.name: Trullo
entries.purpose: dwelling and field store of smallholder farmers in the Valle d'Itria
parts: square plan topped by a conical roof
thick drystone walls (1–2 m)
conical roof of corbelled stone slabs
painted symbols on the pinnacle (protective)
sometimes multiple cones joined into a complex
layout: one square room with central hearth, one side opening per cone
often a two-room pair: trullo grande + trullino
built clustered for farming hamlets
entries.found: Valle d'Itria, Puglia; the trulli town of Alberobello is a UNESCO World Heritage Site
entries.notes: No mortar at all: corbelled cones of limestone, removable on the old tax-dodging story. Corbelled roof, not an arch — every slab is wedged by the ones above.

entries.name: Canal house (Amsterdam)
materials: natural stone pilasters and gable trim
entries.purpose: dwelling and business for merchants and shipping factors
parts: tall narrow gable (step, bell or spout type)
hoist beam (hijsbalk) projecting at the top of the gable
steep internal staircase
cellar for storage, shop/office on the ground floor
large windows, often with shutters inside and out
layout: shop/office below, family above, attic for storage
one room wide, deep; staircase at the back or middle
goods hoisted through the gable because stairs and streets are too steep and narrow
entries.found: Amsterdam's Canal Belt (Grachtengordel), and later Deventer, Haarlem and Utrecht
entries.notes: Width was taxed — hence tall and thin. The hoisting beam at the gable top is the working heart of the facade: bales and barrels came in that way, not through the stairs.

entries.name: Hanseatic merchant's house
entries.purpose: dwelling, office (kontoor) and small warehouse of a trading merchant
parts: crow-stepped gable facing the street
brick facade with blind arches and moulded trim
stone inscription tablet with house name
warehouse courtyard behind
layout: front house: family and kontoor; courtyard; rear house: warehouse
basement vaults for bulk goods; upper floors for living and counting rooms
all trades under one roof, separated by function, not by street
entries.found: Lübeck, Stralsund, Gdańsk, Riga, Tallinn, Deventer, and other Hanseatic core towns
entries.notes: The brick gable is the signature: a skyline of steps announcing each house. Even where the building is a shop today, the gable keeps the memory.

entries.name: Craftsman bungalow
materials: tapered porch columns (brick, stone or wood)
entries.purpose: affordable, mass-market American middle-class dwelling
parts: low-pitched gabled roof with overhanging eaves and exposed rafters
wide front porch with tapered columns on thick piers
built-in cabinetry and benches
open living and dining space (few formal parlours)
exposed beams, earthy palettes
layout: one to one-and-a-half storeys; porch across the front
entry → big living room; kitchen at the back; bedrooms off
ideal for narrow in-town plots
entries.found: US cities and streetcar suburbs; sold widely as plans and kit homes (Sears, Montgomery Ward)
entries.notes: A house designed to be affordable: no basement in many, no parlour, no fuss. Its reaction against Victorian ornament is the whole style.

entries.name: Shotgun house
entries.purpose: affordable single-family dwelling for working people in the South
parts: very narrow rectangle, one room wide
rooms in a straight line front to back — no hallway
front porch with posts
pier-and-beam raised floor
gable end facing the street
layout: front porch → front room → middle room → kitchen at the back
bedroom doors open into rooms, not corridors
side alleys between houses for air
entries.found: New Orleans and the Gulf and southern US; long narrow blocks of lots
entries.notes: The name is likely a Haitian remodeling of 'to-gun' (place of assembly) rather than literally a bullet flying through. Cheap, cool, and the front door is the only door.

entries.name: Queenslander
entries.purpose: single-family dwelling in hot, humid, termite and flood country
parts: raised on hardwood stumps (airflow below, flood safety)
wide verandas on one or more sides
steep roof for heat and rain run-off
timber stairs to the veranda
lattice work under the verandas (air, snakes)
layout: rooms on both sides of a central hall
veranda wraps the house in shade; rooms open to it
kitchen often detached or in the back corner (fire risk)
entries.found: Queensland and northern New South Wales, Australia; best-preserved historic suburbs around Brisbane
entries.notes: A house designed for the sun: floor in the air, shade all around, and airflow everywhere. Tall verandas with turned posts are its signature — it outsold brick in a pre-air-conditioning world.

entries.name: Sod house (soddie)
materials: prairie sod bricks cut from the ground
brushwood or plank roof covered in more sod
entries.purpose: emergency first shelter of prairie homesteaders; later replaced by timber
parts: walls of sod bricks, up to a metre thick
flat or low-pitched earth roof
small timber door and window frames
no interior finish
sod began to grow grass inside when damp
layout: one or two rooms, dark inside
insects and mice shared the living space
roof heavy: posts inside to hold it up

layer 1: e e e e e e|e e . e e e|e e e e e e|e e e e e e|e e e e e e
legend: s sod wall, d door, e earth roof with smoke hole, . air
entries.found: the Great Plains of Nebraska, Kansas, the Dakotas, Oklahoma and the Canadian Prairies
entries.notes: Built from the grassland itself the moment the homesteader arrived — no need to wait for freight. Cool in summer, hot in winter, and damp: one heavy rain and the roof rained inward.

entries.name: Turf house (torfbær)
entries.purpose: dwelling of Icelandic farm families, pole-and-turf construction for treeless terrain
parts: grass-covered roof blending into the ground
double wall: stone inner, earth/turf outer
rafters and driftwood for the frame
baðstofa (heated living/sleeping chamber)
communal hearth with open smoke vent
layout: long range of rooms: storeroom, baðstofa (living), kitchen, loft
children slept in the baðstofa loft
cold ends for storage; warm core for the family
entries.found: Iceland and, earlier, Greenland and Norse settlements on the periphery
entries.notes: Nearly invisible from a distance; the roof is a meadow. Without imported timber or stone, turf over sod is the only reliable warm wall — still standing after a millennium.

entries.name: Yaodong (loess cave dwelling)
cultures: Chinese (Han, especially Jin and Hui regions)
materials: loess carved from cliffs, or pits dug in flat ground
entries.purpose: permanent rural dwelling in the Loess Plateau's dry, cave-stable earth
parts: arched cave rooms off a cliff face or around a sunken courtyard
arched brick facade with lattice doors and windows
sunken courtyard (pit yard) in flat terrain
internal walls plastered white with lime
layout: three caves around a courtyard; back cave main room, side caves for storage and livestock
sunken version: a square pit with cave entrances on all four walls
each courtyard a self-contained homestead
entries.found: Loess Plateau (Henan, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Gansu, Ningxia); 30–40 million people still lived in yaodongs in the early 2000s
entries.notes: Earth itself is the material: no wood, no fired brick. 300 m-high sheer cliffs become ready-made apartment blocks. 1556 Shaanxi earthquake killed ~100,000 largely when yaodongs collapsed.

entries.name: Longhouse (viking/iron age)
materials: wattle and daub or turf walls
entries.purpose: combined dwelling, byre, workshop and storage for the whole farmstead
parts: long rectangular hall (20–45 m)
central hearth, smoke vent in the roof
byre at one or both ends (cattle)
living room in the middle, sometimes a separate kitchen
turf walls on stone foundations
layout: people at one end, cattle at the other, hearth and fire in the middle
long benches along the walls; beds in the side bays
boats stored in separate sheds — never in the longhouse
entries.found: Scandinavia, Iceland, the Faroe Islands, and Viking Age settlements (L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland; Dublin's Wood Quay)
entries.notes: One building is the whole farm: family, guests, animals, grain and tools all under one roof. The famous reconstruction at L'Anse aux Meadows is the only confirmed Viking building in North America.

entries.name: Pile dwelling (palafitte)
entries.purpose: dwelling of a lakeside farming community, raised over shallow water for defence and sanitation
parts: dozens of oak piles driven into the lakebed
raised timber platform at walking-out height above water
small pitched-roof huts on the platform
jetty and palisade
village layout of lanes between houses
layout: platform village over shallow water, ladder or gangplank access
houses in rows on the platform; refuse dropped into the lake below (archaeological gold)
palisade ring around the platform
entries.found: Alpine lakeshores — Lake Zurich, Lake Garda, Lake Geneva, Lake Ohrid; UNESCO World Heritage sites
entries.notes: A prehistoric village on stilts. The pile fields preserved so much organic material that archaeologists reconstruct diet, weaving, even baskets. Burned and rebuilt on the same site repeatedly.

entries.name: Crannog
entries.era: Neolithic to c. 1600 (peak Iron Age and early medieval)
entries.purpose: fortified lake dwelling — a refuge, high-status home, and defensive stronghold
parts: artificial island (round or oval) in a loch or lough
timber palisade around the islet
roundhouse on the islet: timber ring beam, turf or thatch
causeway (often submerged or hidden) linking to the shore
boat shelter
layout: one roundhouse dominates the islet; yard and palisade in front
access by boat or hidden causeway
islets sit in lochs with firm access only under low water
entries.found: Scotland and Ireland; hundreds survive as reed-covered islets in lochs; most studied in Perthshire and the Irish midlands
entries.notes: Scotland and Ireland together have more crannogs than any other country. Originally defensive strongholds of local chiefs; later status symbols and sometimes refuges for outlawed clans.

entries.name: Bothy (mountain shelter)
entries.purpose: simple free shelter for hillwalkers and shepherds — not a dwelling, but a storm refuge
parts: one bare room
stone-built, often at a remote glen head
open fireplace or pot-belly stove (modern refits)
sleeping platform or space for roll mats
no running water, no services
layout: one room; hearth at the back, sleeping space at the front
hut open to all walkers; clean it and carry out what you carry in
built for shepherds and deerstalkers, now maintained by the Mountain Bothies Association
entries.found: Scottish Highlands and Islands; a handful in Wales and England (e.g., in remotest uplands)
entries.notes: A Stone Age shell still in use: drystone, cold, dark, and lifesaving. A bothy is the simplest roof standing between a walker and a Highland night.

entries.name: Cise (Ainu house)
entries.purpose: dwelling of an Ainu extended-family household
parts: low gabled grass house
sunken hearth in the centre
east-facing door (toward the rising sun)
sacred corner for inau (carved ritual twigs)
no windows; smoke exits through gaps in the roof
layout: one long rectangular room; hearth in the middle, family sleeping around it
sacred side to the east; bear-skull pole placement per tradition
annex for winter (sak or indoor storehouse)
entries.found: Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands; best seen today in reconstructed villages (Kotan-Chise, Hokkaido)
entries.notes: A door that faces the sunrise is the whole house — east-facing is law, not preference. The smoke-dried thatch and eternal hearth made the cise a warm, breathable oven in a harsh winter.

entries.name: Geodesic dome house
materials: plywood, concrete or sprayed cellulose infill
entries.purpose: mass-produced affordable housing, marketed as the future of shelter
parts: triangulated shell (buckminster fuller design)
single open interior, no load-bearing walls
skylight at the crown
strong shape, minimal material, excellent load path
self-supporting without columns
layout: open plan; partitions are light and movable
mezzanine or loft platform common
doors and windows are penetrations in the shell
entries.found: experimental and countercultural communities worldwide; dome homes cluster in back-to-the-land tracts and intentional communities
entries.notes: Buckminster Fuller's patented shell: more enclosed volume per unit of material than any rectilinear house. Awkward to partition, awkward to roof, awkward to buy furniture for — and strangely loved.

entries.name: Narrowboat (canal boat)
entries.purpose: cargo or passenger boat on British canals; today a popular permanent or part-time floating home
parts: long flat-bottomed hull, 2.08–2.13 m maximum beam
cabin with galley and beds
rear steering deck with tiller
cratch (bow cover) and butt lee boards
roses and castles paintwork on traditional boats
layout: bow cratch → galley → dining → sleeping cabins → stern steering deck
one corridor, one door on each side
72 ft maximum length, 6 ft 10 in beam to fit narrow locks

entries.found: English and Welsh canals; especially the Grand Union, Leeds and Liverpool, Kennet and Avon and the Trent and Mersey
entries.notes: Locks 7 ft wide dictate everything: 2.08 m beam, 22 m long, tiller steering, flat bottom. About 8,500 are registered permanent homes today — a floating village that moves.
